sentences.text: A short, blade-like crest sits below the front of the lower jaws.

The tooth sockets are raised above the roof of the mouth and the jaw edge, measuring no more than four millimeters across. These sockets are spaced exactly as wide as they are deep, creating a density of about six sockets for every three centimeters of jaw margin.
The center line of the palate is also raised, while the lower jaw features a distinct crest on its lower section.
This species is defined by a unique mix of features, including a crested snout, a rounded snout tip, a rounded lower jaw front, and diverging front tooth sockets.
James Scott Bowerbank named and described the species in 1846 using fossils from a limestone quarry near Maidstone in Kent.
In 1914, Reginald Walter Hooley moved the species into a new genus called Lonchodectes, which translates to 'the spear-biter'.
The original species name, Pterodactylus giganteus, became the type species for the new genus Lonchodraco.
Bowerbank originally estimated that this giant creature had a wingspan between 2.4 and 2.7 meters.
In 2013, Rodrigues and Kellner placed Lonchodraco in the family Lonchodraconidae, noting that it was the only member of that group.
Later research by Pêgas and colleagues recovered the genus within Lonchodraconidae as the sister group to Ikrandraco.

Two other species formerly in Lonchodectes were transferred to Lonchodraco, becoming L. machaerorhynchus and L. microdon, though the question mark in the latter name shows authors are unsure about this placement.
Rodrigues and Kellner viewed Lonchodraco as a clade defined by shared derived traits that separate it from related groups.
This pterodactyloid pterosaur lived during the Early and Late Cretaceous in southern England.
The type specimen was discovered in the Chalk Formation, which dates from the Cenomanian to Turonian stages.
The animal lived from the Valanginian to the Turonian, spanning from 137.05 to 89.8 million years ago.
Averianov (2020) challenged the classification of Lonchodraco, suggesting that L. machaerorhynchus belongs in the genus Ikrandraco and that L. microdon is a junior synonym.

The type specimen of Ornithocheirus oweni was referred to L. microdon in the same study where Lonchodraco was named, following David Unwin's 2001 conclusions, implying this species might be a more modern synonym.
